title: The ladder (Genesis 28:10–22)
hookLine: a runaway sleeps on a stone and wakes saying the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not

lines: THE BLESSING, AND A BROTHER'S RAGE.
ALONE IN THE HILLS AT SUNSET.
cards: Jacob has the blessing. He also has a brother who wants him dead. So he leaves home with almost nothing, walking toward Haran, his uncle's country, alone.
By sunset he's somewhere in the hills: no inn, no friend, no tent. He puts a stone under his head and lies down on the ground.
A night far from home, in a bus station or a strange city, after something you did went badly wrong: that's this night. It's the last place anyone expects to meet God.

teach.b: First, the dream. A ladder, or a stairway, stands on the earth, its top reaching heaven, and the angels of God are going up and down on it. Going up first, then down, as if they were already here.
And the Lord stands above it. Second, the promise. God doesn't scold Jacob for the lie.
God repeats the promise to Abraham: the land, descendants like the dust of the earth, and in you all the families of the earth will be blessed.
Then something new, just for him: I will keep you wherever you go, and I will not leave you. Third, the waking.

In the Douay-Rheims: "And when Jacob awaked out of sleep, he said: Indeed the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not." Then, trembling: "this is no other but the house of God, and the gate of heaven."
He sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and calls the place Bethel, Hebrew for house of God. A nowhere place in the hills, renamed. Fourth, where the Church hears it.
In the Gospel of John, Jesus tells Nathanael he'll see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
Christian tradition reads Christ as the ladder itself, the meeting of heaven and earth.
And in the Church's traditional chant for the dedication of a church, the Mass opens with Jacob's words in Latin: Terribilis est locus iste, how awesome is this place.
A building, consecrated with the words of a runaway who slept on a rock.

how: The traditional entrance chant for the dedication of a church, Terribilis est locus iste, takes Jacob's words at Bethel, and Genesis 28:11–18 is among the readings the Church offers for that rite.

Jacob dreams at a well-known shrine
he's nowhere in particular, sleeping on a stone. he renames the place Bethel.

games.q: you're Jacob, a runaway, waking on a stone after a dream of angels and God's promise. what do you say?
o: indeed the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not.
I'll go home and make it right with Esau.
games.why: "Indeed the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not." then he calls it the house of God and the gate of heaven, and names it Bethel.

practice: Think back over the past week for a place you passed through without a thought: a waiting room, a sink full of dishes, a sleepless hour.

Replay it slowly, as if it were Bethel, and look for what you missed: a kindness, a quiet, a person, a gift. If you pray, say Jacob's words about it, the Lord was in this place; if not, simply notice what was there.

wordCard.voice: The ladder. Jacob's dream at Bethel: a stairway between earth and heaven, angels on it, God above, and a promise: I will not leave you.

orig.note: Hebrew: Bethel, house of God. Jacob's name for the place he slept on a stone.

carryVoice: Your line: and I knew it not. Even a stone pillow can lie at heaven's gate. Until tomorrow, then.
